meta.title: Connective Tissue
meta.summary: Connective tissue is the most diverse and abundant tissue in the body, found in skin, membranes, muscles, bones, nerves, and all internal organs. It is...

blocks.x: Connective tissue is the most diverse and abundant tissue in the body, found in skin, membranes, muscles, bones, nerves, and all internal organs. It is highly vascular, with two notable exceptions: cartilage (avascular) and tendons (scanty blood supply). Except for cartilage, connective tissues are also supplied with nerves.

blocks.name: Functions of connective tissue
blocks.def: Holds internal organs together and gives them shape; connects tissues to each other; forms a supporting framework for the body; transports substances throughout the body; defends against microbes and other invaders; stores nutrients as fat.

blocks.x: Connective tissue is composed of an extracellular matrix (ECM) — made of ground substance and fibers — plus its resident and transient cells.

blocks.name: Ground substance
blocks.def: A colourless, transparent, gel-like material in which the cells and fibers of connective tissue are embedded — a complex mixture of glycosaminoglycans (mucopolysaccharides), proteoglycans, and glycoproteins. Serves as a lubricant, resists compressive forces, facilitates diffusion of substances, acts as a barrier, and holds body fluids. May be fluid, semifluid, gelatinous, or calcified.

blocks.name: <term d="A strong rope-like protein fibre that gives tissues their tensile strength.">Collagen</term> fibres
blocks.def: The most abundant protein type, found in nearly all connective tissue (at least 25 different types exist). Exhibit great tensile strength; most concentrated where strong support is needed. Do not branch.

blocks.name: Reticular fibres
blocks.def: Composed of type III collagen. Form a delicate, net-like supporting framework in the liver, lymph nodes, spleen, and hemopoietic organs; stain black with silver. Support capillaries, nerve, and muscle cells.

blocks.name: Elastic fibres
blocks.def: Made of the protein <term d="A stretchy protein fibre that lets tissue recoil back into shape after being stretched.">elastin</term> surrounded by the glycoprotein fibrillin. Thin, small, and branching; recoil to their original size after stretching. Needed wherever stretching without breaking is essential — lung, skin, bladder, and large blood vessels like the aorta.

blocks.name: Scurvy
blocks.def: A disease caused by defective collagen formation from vitamin C deficiency, resulting in loose teeth, skin haemorrhages, and (if untreated) death.

blocks.name: Collagen type I
blocks.def: Found in bones and tendons.

blocks.name: Collagen type II
blocks.def: Found in cartilage (hyaline and elastic).

blocks.name: Collagen type III
blocks.def: Forms reticular fibres.

blocks.name: Collagen type IV
blocks.def: Found in the <term d="The thin supporting layer on which an epithelium sits, separating it from the tissue beneath.">basement membrane</term>.

blocks.name: Collagen type V
blocks.def: Found in blood vessels.

blocks.x: Connective tissue cells fall into two broad groups:

blocks.name: Resident (fixed) cells
blocks.def: Fibroblasts, fixed macrophages, adipocytes, mast cells, adult stem cells.

blocks.name: Wandering (transient) cells
blocks.def: Lymphocytes, plasma cells, neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, monocytes, and certain macrophages — most migrate in from local blood vessels in response to specific stimuli.

blocks.name: -blast / -cyte / -clast naming
blocks.def: "-blasts" are immature cells that create the matrix; "-cytes" are mature cells that maintain the matrix; "-clasts" break the matrix down for remodeling.

blocks.name: Fibroblasts
blocks.def: Fusiform-shaped cells with slender cytoplasmic processes and a large oval nucleus. The most abundant connective tissue cell; synthesizes collagen, elastic, and reticular fibers and secretes the ECM.

blocks.name: Macrophages
blocks.def: Irregularly shaped, phagocytic cells developed from monocytes. Fixed macrophages include alveolar macrophages (lungs) and splenic macrophages; they ingest bacteria and other foreign material.

blocks.name: Plasma cells
blocks.def: Small cells developed from B lymphocytes; secrete antibodies.

blocks.name: Mast cells
blocks.def: Round or fusiform cells that produce histamine (causes blood vessel dilation as part of the inflammatory response) and heparin (prevents blood coagulation).

blocks.name: Adipocytes
blocks.def: Fat cells; store triglycerides.

blocks.x: Connective tissue is classified into three main groups based on the relative amounts of cells, fibers, and ground substance present:

blocks.name: The three classes of connective tissue
blocks.def: 1) Embryonic connective tissue (mesenchyme and mucous tissue). 2) Connective tissue proper (the "mature" loose and dense connective tissues). 3) Specialized connective tissue (cartilage, bone, and blood).

blocks.x: Some connective tissues — bone, areolar connective tissue, dense irregular connective tissue, and blood — regenerate relatively easily.

blocks.name: Mesenchyme
blocks.def: Irregularly (stellate) shaped mesenchymal cells embedded in a semifluid ground substance containing delicate reticular fibers. Gives rise to the various connective tissues of the body; found in the developing embryo/fetus. Its low collagen content matches the limited physical stress on the growing fetus.

blocks.name: Mucous connective tissue (Wharton's jelly)
blocks.def: Widely scattered fibroblasts embedded in a viscous, jelly-like ground substance containing fine collagen fibers. Found in the umbilical cord.

blocks.x: Connective tissue proper has two subclasses:

blocks.name: Loose connective tissue
blocks.def: Few fibers, abundant cells of various types, and abundant ground substance. Includes areolar, adipose, and reticular tissue.

blocks.name: Dense connective tissue
blocks.def: Abundant fibers, few cells, and little ground substance. Includes dense irregular (the most common type), dense regular, and elastic connective tissue.

blocks.name: Areolar connective tissue
blocks.def: The most widely distributed connective tissue type, and considered the "model" connective tissue — abundant ground substance and fibroblasts, fewer fibers (collagen fibers dominate, though reticular and elastic fibers may be present). Found underlying epithelial tissue (as the lamina propria), surrounding small nerves and blood vessels, and packaging organs throughout the body.

blocks.name: <term d="Fat tissue — connective tissue packed with cells that store energy and insulate.">Adipose tissue</term>
blocks.def: Composed of adipocytes specialized for fat storage, with cytoplasm and nucleus pushed to one side by the fat droplet.

blocks.name: Yellow (white) adipose tissue
blocks.def: The most abundant adipose type in adults; white at birth, yellows with age.

blocks.name: Brown adipose tissue
blocks.def: Found mainly in the fetus/infant, with small adult amounts in the axillae, neck, and near the kidneys. Appears darker due to a rich blood supply and numerous pigmented mitochondria — generates less ATP but more heat, helping maintain body temperature.

blocks.cap: Adipose tissue — adipocytes with fat droplets pushing the cytoplasm and nucleus to the cell periphery.

blocks.name: Reticular connective tissue
blocks.def: A network of reticular fibers (a thin form of type III collagen) and reticular cells. Forms the stroma (supporting framework) of the liver, spleen, and lymph nodes, and is also found in red bone marrow. Functions include binding smooth muscle cells and filtering out worn-out blood cells (spleen) or microbes (lymph nodes).

blocks.name: Dense irregular connective tissue
blocks.def: Thick, densely packed collagen fibers arranged irregularly (random orientation), with fewer cells/ground substance/elastic fibers than loose CT. Found in the dermis, digestive tract submucosa, <term d="The tough membrane wrapping the outer surface of a bone, carrying its blood supply.">periosteum</term>, perichondrium, fibrous joint capsules, and organ capsules (lymph nodes, spleen, testes, liver). Function: withstands tension from multiple directions, providing structural strength.

blocks.name: Dense regular connective tissue
blocks.def: Similar composition to dense irregular, but collagen fibers are arranged in regular, compact, parallel bundles, with loose CT (and rows of fibroblasts) between bundles. Found wherever strong tensile strength in one direction is needed — tendons, ligaments, and aponeuroses.

blocks.name: Elastic connective tissue
blocks.def: Elastic fibers predominate, with fibroblasts between them; unstained tissue appears yellowish. Function: allows recoil after stretching. Found in lung tissue, the walls of elastic arteries, the trachea, bronchial tubes, true vocal cords, and some intervertebral ligaments.

blocks.name: Cartilage
blocks.def: A specialized dense connective tissue made of cells (chondrocytes) and a highly specialized extracellular matrix (≈95% of the tissue, 60–80% water). The matrix is solid and firm but flexible. Cartilage is avascular — nutrient diffusion between blood vessels in the surrounding tissue and the embedded chondrocytes is possible because of a high ratio of glycosaminoglycans to type II collagen fibers. Supports soft tissues and assists long-bone growth; more abundant in the embryo than in the adult.

blocks.name: Chondrogenic cells
blocks.def: Stem cells for cartilage.

blocks.name: Chondroblasts
blocks.def: Cartilage-forming cells; produce and secrete the ECM.

blocks.name: Chondrocytes
blocks.def: Mature cartilage cells embedded within lacunae in the matrix; maintain the ECM.

blocks.name: Chondroclasts
blocks.def: Resorb calcified cartilage, which is then replaced by bone.

blocks.name: Hyaline cartilage
blocks.def: The most common cartilage type ("hyaline" = glassy), made of abundant type II collagen, with chondrocytes arranged singly or in clusters (isogenous groups), and a surrounding perichondrium. Provides support through flexibility and resilience, and resists repetitive/compressive stress; serves as a temporary fetal skeleton before replacement by bone. Found in: the fetal skeleton, articular cartilage of synovial joints, costal cartilage, epiphyseal growth plates, and the nasal septum, tracheal rings, bronchi, and larynx.

blocks.name: Elastic cartilage
blocks.def: Similar to hyaline cartilage but with abundant yellow elastic fibers and a random arrangement of chondrocytes; perichondrium present. Maintains the shape of a structure while allowing great flexibility/repeated bending, and never calcifies. Found in the external ear (pinna), epiglottis, auditory tube, external auditory canal, and parts of the larynx.

blocks.cap: Elastic cartilage — note the dense network of elastic fibers among the chondrocytes.

blocks.name: Fibrocartilage
blocks.def: Structurally intermediate between hyaline cartilage and dense connective tissue. Chondrocytes are arranged in parallel rows (singly or in isogenous groups) between bundles of collagen (type I); lacks a perichondrium. Provides tensile strength and shock-absorbing capacity. Found in the anulus fibrosus of intervertebral discs, the pubic symphysis, and the menisci and labra of the knee/shoulder/hip joints.

blocks.name: Perichondrium
blocks.def: A dense irregular connective tissue layer surrounding hyaline and elastic cartilage (except at articular surfaces), made of an outer fibrous layer and an inner cellular layer containing chondrogenic cells and chondroblasts. Provides oxygen/nutrients (via its own blood vessels) to the avascular cartilage below, supplies new chondrocytes for growth/repair, and resists outward expansion of the cartilage under pressure.

blocks.name: Appositional growth
blocks.def: "Surface growth" — chondrogenic cells in the perichondrium differentiate into chondroblasts, adding new cartilage tissue at the periphery.

blocks.name: Interstitial growth
blocks.def: "Internal growth" — pre-existing chondrocytes within the cartilage divide and synthesize new matrix; occurs only during early cartilage formation, in articular cartilage, and at the epiphyseal plates. Cartilage stops growing in the late teens as the skeleton stops growing, and chondrocytes cease dividing — which is why cartilage regenerates poorly in adults.

blocks.x: Cartilage cells can give rise to benign (chondroma) or malignant (chondrosarcoma) tumors. Calcification of cartilage matrix is a normal part of bone growth in children, but in adults it is a sign of aging — note that calcified cartilage is still not bone.
Bone itself is classed as a specialized connective tissue, and is highly vascular (unlike cartilage).

blocks.name: Bone composition
blocks.def: About 35% organic components by dry weight (cells, collagen fibers — 95% of the organic fraction — and ground substance), and about 65% inorganic (calcified) components: calcium, phosphate, bicarbonate, citrate, magnesium, potassium, and sodium, primarily as hydroxyapatite crystals, Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2.

blocks.name: Osteoprogenitor (osteogenic) cells
blocks.def: Stem cells located in the periosteum and <term d="The thin lining on the inner surfaces of bone, facing the marrow cavity.">endosteum</term> that persist throughout life and can be activated for bone repair after fractures.

blocks.name: Osteoblasts (bone connective tissue view)
blocks.def: Produce new bone matrix through <term d="The process by which new bone is formed.">ossification</term>, eventually becoming trapped within their own secreted matrix in a lacuna.

blocks.name: Osteocytes (bone connective tissue view)
blocks.def: Mature, non-dividing bone cells housed in lacunae; maintain the bone matrix, with cytoplasmic extensions passing through canaliculi in the lamellae to connect with neighbouring osteocytes.

blocks.name: Osteoclasts (bone connective tissue view)
blocks.def: Large, motile, multinucleated cells that resorb bone by secreting hydrochloric acid (dissolving the mineral matrix) and lysosomal enzymes (digesting the organic matrix), releasing calcium and other minerals.

blocks.name: Compact (dense) bone
blocks.def: About 80% of the skeleton by mass; made of osteons (Haversian systems) with little space between them; almost entirely lamellar (mature) bone; the strongest bone form, providing protection, support, and stress resistance.

blocks.name: Lacunae & canaliculi
blocks.def: Lacunae are tiny cavities between lamellae where osteocytes reside; canaliculi are narrow passageways connecting neighbouring lacunae, carrying the cytoplasmic extensions that let osteocytes communicate with one another.

blocks.name: Perforating (Volkmann's) canals
blocks.def: Canals running at right angles to the central (Haversian) canals, connecting the periosteum's blood/nerve supply to that of the central canals and the marrow cavity.

blocks.name: Interstitial lamellae
blocks.def: Groups of incomplete lamellae lying between osteons — the remnants of older osteons that have been partially removed by bone remodeling.

blocks.name: Circumferential lamellae
blocks.def: Lamellae on the external and internal surfaces of <term d="The dense, solid outer layer of bone that gives it strength.">compact bone</term> that help resist twisting forces along the entire long bone.

blocks.name: Periosteum (bone connective tissue view)
blocks.def: A dense irregular connective tissue layer covering the outer surfaces of bone, except at articular surfaces, sesamoid bones, and ossicles. United to the underlying bone by collagen (Sharpey's) fibers; osteogenic and important in fracture repair; richly supplied with pain-sensitive nerve fibers.

blocks.name: Endosteum (bone connective tissue view)
blocks.def: A thin, vascular connective tissue membrane lining the inner (medullary) surface of bone, covering the trabeculae of <term d="The lighter, honeycombed bone found inside the ends of long bones.">spongy bone</term> and lining the central canals of osteons; osteogenic, contributing to new bone formation.

blocks.name: Spongy (cancellous) bone
blocks.def: About 20% of the skeleton; made of an open lattice of trabeculae with spaces filled by red bone marrow, lacking osteons; lighter than compact bone but able to resist stress from multiple directions.

blocks.name: Trabeculae
blocks.def: The interconnected bony spikes/plates that make up spongy bone, oriented along lines of mechanical stress to maximize strength with minimal material.

blocks.name: Central (Haversian) canal
blocks.def: The channel running through the center of each <term d="The cylindrical unit of compact bone built around a central canal carrying vessels.">osteon</term>, carrying blood vessels, nerves, and loose connective tissue.

blocks.name: Lamellae
blocks.def: Concentric rings of calcified bone matrix arranged around the central canal of an osteon, running roughly parallel to the long axis of the bone's <term d="The long shaft of a long bone.">diaphysis</term>.

blocks.name: Chondroma vs. chondrosarcoma
blocks.def: Chondroma is a benign tumor arising from cartilage cells; chondrosarcoma is the malignant counterpart.
